tip: 'De lo que' = about which (abstract): 'de lo que hablamos' = what we talked about. Neuter 'lo' for ideas, not physical objects.
'Decepcionado' looks like deceived but means disappointed – nobody lied, they just let you down. Actual deception is 'engaño'; 'decepción' is dashed hopes.
'Cuyo hijo', not 'cuya', after 'la mujer': 'cuyo' agrees with the thing owned ('hijo'), never the owner. English whose never budges; Spanish whose bends to what follows.
A 'plantón' is literally a big sapling – planted and left standing. 'Me han dado un plantón' = they planted you like a tree and walked off: stood up.
English asks people TO do things; Spanish can't. 'Les pedí que vinieran' – after 'pedir' you need a full que-clause, never an infinitive for another person.
'He perdido' today – in Spain. Spaniards use the perfect for anything from today; most of Latin America says 'perdí' even for five minutes ago. Both are correct.
'Ha aprobado' isn't 'has approved' – 'aprobar un examen' means to PASS it. The examiner approves your answers, so YOU 'aprobar' the exam.
'Habrá olvidado' isn't a prediction – future tenses double as guesses about the present. 'Se habrá olvidado' = he MUST have forgotten.
Trap: 'cierto' means 'true,' yet 'por cierto' isn't 'for certain' – it signals a topic swerve, 'by the way.' To actually say 'certainly,' you'd want 'sin duda'.
'Ojalá' comes from Arabic 'law sha'a Allah', if God wills – a holdover from Moorish Spain, hence the subjunctive 'hubiera' in every wish.
'Hemos vuelto a cometer' isn't about returning anywhere. 'Volver a' + infinitive = do it AGAIN – Spanish 're-does' actions by 'returning to' them.
Why the extra 'la'? When the object moves up front – 'La casa... LA han derribado' – Spanish must echo it with a pronoun. English fronts silently; Spanish leaves a marker.
'Como si' always takes past subjunctive – 'como si fuera' – even when English happily says 'as if it IS'. No exceptions.
Never 'si tendría'! After 'si', Spanish bans the conditional: 'si tuviera... viajaría'. The '-ra' form belongs in the if-half, '-ría' in the result.
Wait – future after 'si'? 'Si aceptaré' is legal because this 'si' means 'whether', not 'if'. Only condition-si bans the future; whether-si allows any tense.
Ten years HAVE passed – pure fact. But 'hayan pasado' goes subjunctive anyway: 'es increíble que' filters the fact through your amazement, and feelings trigger subjunctive.
'Nunca... nada' – a double negative, and it's mandatory. Spanish negatives must agree: once 'nunca' opens the sentence, 'anything' becomes 'nada', never 'algo'.
'Contigo' is a Latin fossil: 'tecum' meant 'you-with,' Spanish bolted 'con' onto the front, and the old 'cum' melted into the final '-go'. 'Conmigo' hides the same relic.
English drops the 'on' in 'insisted (on) that...'; Spanish never does: 'insistió EN que'. Verbs keep their preposition even before a whole que-clause.
'Esperaba' is three English verbs at once: hope, wait, expect. 'Esperaba que me llamaran' = I hoped they'd call – context, not the verb, tells you which.
'Tan pronto como crucemos' – not 'cruzamos'. Time clauses about the future take subjunctive; English hides the not-yet-real behind plain present ('as soon as we cross').
'Habíamos quedado' isn't about staying. Plain 'quedar' = arrange to meet ('we'd agreed on eight'); 'quedarse', with the reflexive, = stay.
The deadline word is 'para': 'para las diez' means 'BY ten,' a finish line. 'Habré terminado' plus 'para' is how Spanish promises something done before a set time.
'De ahí que' – literally 'from there that' – means 'that's why', yet oddly demands subjunctive: 'decidiera'. The result is real, but the formula is fixed.
'De haber' + participle is a formal alternative to 'si hubiéramos' + participle for past unreal conditions.
'Hubiera invertido' is the past unrealized condition; 'sería' gives the present hypothetical result – a mixed conditional.
'Si bien' isn't 'if well' – it's a formal 'although', and unlike conditional 'si' it takes plain indicative: 'si bien el hotel era caro'. No hypothesis in sight.
English has one 'but'; Spanish splits it. After a negative like 'no solo', it must be 'sino', never 'pero' – 'pero' contradicts, 'sino' replaces or piles on. Here it stacks a second complaint.
'Se ha demostrado' = It has been shown. Impersonal 'se' works in all tenses: 'se ha dicho que...' = It has been said that...
'Confío en que' + indicative 'logrará': trust asserts rather than doubts, so no subjunctive needed – unlike 'dudo que', which always flips it.
